title: DPF Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1
shortDescription: Diesel particulate filter efficiency or bypass fault: dpf efficiency below threshold bank 1.
fullDescription: The PCM monitors DPF performance using upstream and downstream pressure and temperature sensors. DPF Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1 indicates the filter is not trapping or regenerating particulates within calibrated limits, or the bypass mechanism (where equipped) is not in the commanded position.
safetyImpact: Continued driving may force the engine into limp mode and risks permanent DPF damage from excessive soot loading.

causes.cause: Excessive soot or ash loading in DPF

fixSteps.title: Scan and Read DPF Live Data
fixSteps.instruction: Connect a scan tool capable of reading diesel-specific PIDs. Record DPF differential pressure, soot load, ash load, exhaust temperatures upstream and downstream, and last regeneration distance.

fixSteps.title: Inspect DPF and Sensors
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the DPF body, differential pressure tubing, and exhaust gas temperature sensors for cracks, soot leaks, kinked tubes, or damaged wiring.

fixSteps.title: Attempt Forced Regeneration
fixSteps.instruction: Using the scan tool, command a stationary or driving regeneration per OEM procedure. Monitor exhaust gas temperatures and soot load reduction.

fixSteps.title: Clean or Replace DPF
fixSteps.instruction: If regeneration fails or ash load is excessive, remove the DPF for off-vehicle thermal/aqueous cleaning, or replace with an OEM unit. Reset adaptations.

faq.q: Can I drive with a DPF efficiency code?
faq.a: Only briefly. A loaded DPF builds backpressure that damages turbos and pistons. Address it promptly.

faq.q: Is forced regeneration safe?
faq.a: Yes when performed per OEM procedure with the vehicle in a well-ventilated outdoor area away from flammables.

faq.q: Why does my DPF keep clogging?
faq.a: Short trips, excessive idling, EGR faults, and failing injectors all cause excess soot. Fix the upstream cause or the new DPF will fail too.

title: DPF Pressure Sensor A Circuit
shortDescription: Diesel particulate filter differential pressure or regeneration fault: dpf pressure sensor a circuit.
fullDescription: The PCM uses the differential pressure sensor across the DPF to estimate soot load and trigger regeneration. DPF Pressure Sensor A Circuit indicates a circuit, range, or performance condition that prevents accurate soot estimation or successful regeneration.
safetyImpact: Risk of limp mode and DPF substrate damage if not corrected. No immediate driving hazard.

causes.cause: Clogged or kinked pressure sensor sample tubes

fixSteps.title: Scan and Read DPF Live Data
fixSteps.instruction: Connect a scan tool capable of reading diesel-specific PIDs. Record DPF differential pressure, soot load, ash load, exhaust temperatures upstream and downstream, and last regeneration distance.

fixSteps.title: Inspect DPF and Sensors
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the DPF body, differential pressure tubing, and exhaust gas temperature sensors for cracks, soot leaks, kinked tubes, or damaged wiring.

fixSteps.title: Attempt Forced Regeneration
fixSteps.instruction: Using the scan tool, command a stationary or driving regeneration per OEM procedure. Monitor exhaust gas temperatures and soot load reduction.

fixSteps.title: Replace DPF Pressure Sensor and Tubes
fixSteps.instruction: Replace the differential pressure sensor and inspect/replace the sample tubes. Tubes must be free of soot and not kinked. Clear adaptations and re-run regeneration.

faq.q: Can I just delete the DPF?
faq.a: No. DPF deletion is illegal in most jurisdictions and voids emissions warranties.

faq.q: How often should DPF regenerate?
faq.a: Passive regeneration occurs continuously at highway loads; active regeneration every 200–500 miles is normal.

faq.q: Is sensor replacement enough?
faq.a: Often yes for a circuit code, but a high-soot code requires forced regeneration or DPF cleaning as well.

title: DPF Differential Pressure Too High
shortDescription: Diesel particulate filter differential pressure or regeneration fault: dpf differential pressure too high.
fullDescription: The PCM uses the differential pressure sensor across the DPF to estimate soot load and trigger regeneration. DPF Differential Pressure Too High indicates a circuit, range, or performance condition that prevents accurate soot estimation or successful regeneration.
safetyImpact: Risk of limp mode and DPF substrate damage if not corrected. No immediate driving hazard.

causes.cause: Clogged or kinked pressure sensor sample tubes

fixSteps.title: Scan and Read DPF Live Data
fixSteps.instruction: Connect a scan tool capable of reading diesel-specific PIDs. Record DPF differential pressure, soot load, ash load, exhaust temperatures upstream and downstream, and last regeneration distance.

fixSteps.title: Inspect DPF and Sensors
fixSteps.instruction: Inspect the DPF body, differential pressure tubing, and exhaust gas temperature sensors for cracks, soot leaks, kinked tubes, or damaged wiring.

fixSteps.title: Attempt Forced Regeneration
fixSteps.instruction: Using the scan tool, command a stationary or driving regeneration per OEM procedure. Monitor exhaust gas temperatures and soot load reduction.

fixSteps.title: Replace DPF Pressure Sensor and Tubes
fixSteps.instruction: Replace the differential pressure sensor and inspect/replace the sample tubes. Tubes must be free of soot and not kinked. Clear adaptations and re-run regeneration.

title: Reductant (DEF) Tank Temperature Sensor Circuit
shortDescription: Diesel exhaust fluid (DEF/AdBlue) temperature or heater fault: reductant (def) tank temperature sensor circuit.
fullDescription: The PCM monitors DEF tank temperature to control tank and line heaters that prevent freezing in cold weather. Reductant (DEF) Tank Temperature Sensor Circuit indicates a sensor or heater fault that may prevent SCR operation when temperatures are low.
safetyImpact: In cold climates, frozen DEF disables SCR and can lead to engine derate or no-start until thawed.

causes.cause: Failed DEF tank or line heater element

symptoms: No-start condition after extended cold soak

fixSteps.title: Scan and Read DPF Live Data
fixSteps.instruction: Connect a scan tool capable of reading diesel-specific PIDs. Record DPF differential pressure, soot load, ash load, exhaust temperatures upstream and downstream, and last regeneration distance.

fixSteps.title: Inspect DEF Tank Wiring
fixSteps.instruction: With ignition off, disconnect the DEF tank header connector and inspect for crystallized DEF (white residue), corrosion, and cracked insulation. Clean carefully with warm distilled water.

fixSteps.title: Test Sensor and Heater Resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Measure DEF tank temperature sensor resistance and compare with spec at known ambient temperature. Measure heater element resistance — typically 1–10 ohms when present.

fixSteps.title: Replace DEF Tank Header
fixSteps.instruction: Drain DEF, remove the tank header, install the new sensor/heater assembly, refill with fresh DEF, and clear codes. Run vehicle until system pressurizes and self-test passes.

faq.q: Will the truck stop if DEF is frozen?
faq.a: Modern systems allow operation while DEF thaws, but persistent SCR faults trigger speed limit and eventually no-start.

faq.q: Can I add hot water to thaw DEF?
faq.a: No — water contaminates DEF. Move the vehicle to a heated space or use the OEM DEF heating procedure.

faq.q: Does brand of DEF matter?
faq.a: Use only API-certified DEF that meets ISO 22241 to avoid contamination and SCR damage.
